strengths: Addresses a practical NLP question: when collecting labels and specializing a smaller model becomes preferable to prompting a general model. Studying intermediate training sizes and variability is a useful empirical contribution.

The evaluation covers eight datasets, eight models, and four approaches. Repeated experiments—100 runs for fine-tuning, 20 for most other settings, and 10 for GPT—provide substantial evidence of variation across tasks and runs.
The manuscript links experimental code and provides prompts, basic training settings, individual-model plots, and explicit limitations, offering a useful foundation for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The headline '100 labels on average' is insufficiently substantiated. The aggregation procedure and weighting are unclear, including whether this means averaging individual break-even points or finding a crossing of averaged curves. Table 1 reports fine-tuning crossings against in-context learning at 9,000 labels for SST2 and 5,000 for BoolQ. These results require more qualified annotation-budget recommendations and a reproducible derivation of the headline statistic.

The second break-even point compares mean minus one standard deviation against mean plus one standard deviation. This is a descriptive heuristic, not a worst-case bound or a calibrated guarantee of low probability of underperformance. Uncertainty in the estimated crossings and treatment of cases without an observed crossing are also missing. These issues weaken the central interpretation of the reported 100–200% increase.

Label accounting and selection procedures are underspecified. Appendix A reserves 20% of the data for validation and uses early stopping without explaining how validation labels enter the annotation budget. The paper also reports the best models, precision settings, and preceding in-context example counts without establishing a clear separation between selection and test evaluation. Consequently, the reported thresholds are not yet established as achievable under the stated label budgets.

Baseline adequacy needs stronger validation. All models use one prompt developed on Mistral, and Table 2 describes BoolQ as determining whether a passage contains an answer, which differs from answering its yes/no question. Ambiguous verbalisers further complicate interpretation. Correct task instructions and a modest prompt robustness check are necessary because baseline quality directly determines the break-even points.

The efficiency and quantization conclusions exceed the supporting analysis. Table 3 lacks the workload assumptions needed to reproduce its compute comparisons across training sizes and inference volumes; bit-width-normalized FLOPs do not establish practical speedups. Figure 6 also shows substantial quantization differences for Zephyr on BoolQ, requiring qualification of the broad claim of negligible impact.

Several explanations remain observational: model size is confounded with architecture and training history, while binary versus multiclass comparisons also change task characteristics. Section 3.1 attributes performance differences to pretraining exposure despite acknowledging that exposure is unknown. Narrower conclusions are warranted. Overall, the baseline and estimation concerns require substantive revision before a sound Findings recommendation; focused corrections and reanalysis could reasonably support resubmission next cycle.
